usage: Used when discussing project management, timelines, or workplace pressure.
alternatives: to get it done by the due date
example_sentences: We are working overtime to meet the deadline for this project.
It is always a challenge to meet a deadline when the requirements keep changing.
The team managed to meet the deadline despite the technical issues.
If we don't meet the deadline, we will lose the client's trust.
Can we realistically meet the deadline by Friday afternoon?
native_notes: We use 'meet' for deadlines, not 'reach'. 'Hit' a deadline is a more informal, dynamic version.

uzbek: ishga ko'milib qolish, juda band bo'lish
usage: Used to describe having an overwhelming amount of work to do.
common_mistakes: I am snowed in my work
alternatives: to be up to my eyes in work
to have a lot on my plate
example_sentences: I'm sorry I can't help you with that report; I'm completely snowed under at the moment.
He has been snowed under with paperwork all week.
Don't expect a reply today, she's absolutely snowed under.
When you're snowed under, it's important to prioritize your tasks.
We're all a bit snowed under during the end-of-year audit.
native_notes: Very common idiomatic way to express that you are too busy. Sounds much more natural than 'I am very busy'.
russian: быть погруженным в работу, быть очень занятым

usage: Describes standard office hours or the traditional corporate work lifestyle.
example_sentences: I've always wanted a creative career rather than just a boring nine-to-five job.
She finds the routine of a nine-to-five job quite comforting.
Is it really a nine-to-five job, or do you have to work weekends too?
He left his nine-to-five to start his own business.
For many, the nine-to-five lifestyle provides a sense of structure.
native_notes: Refers to the stereotypical 9 AM to 5 PM shift. Can be used to imply a routine that some might find dull.

usage: Used in team settings to talk about whether someone is doing their fair share of work.
example_sentences: If everyone pulls their weight, we can finish this project by tomorrow.
She doesn't think her colleague is really pulling his weight.
The manager noticed that some team members weren't pulling their weight.
It's frustrating when you have to pull your weight and others don't.
Our success depends on every person pulling their weight.
collocations: the importance of pulling one's weight
native_notes: Idiom used specifically regarding collaborative effort. You 'pull' it, you don't 'carry' it.

usage: Used when you are too busy with work or tasks to do anything else at the moment.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + tied up + with/doing + something
example_sentences: I'm afraid I'm a bit tied up with a client meeting until five o'clock.
Could we reschedule? I'm completely tied up with this report all morning.
He's tied up at the moment, but he should be free in about twenty minutes.
Sorry for the delay; I was tied up with an urgent issue on the shop floor.
Are you free for a quick coffee? No, I'm tied up with deadlines.
native_notes: Much more common and natural in a professional context than simply saying 'I am busy'.

expression: to keep on top of things
usage: Used to describe staying organized and managing your workload effectively before it becomes overwhelming.
example_sentences: To keep on top of my emails, I check my inbox twice a day.
We need a better project management tool to help us keep on top of our deadlines.
It's difficult to keep on top of things when the team is short-staffed.
She has a very busy schedule, but she always manages to keep on top of things.
Make sure you keep on top of your paperwork before the end of the month.
collocations: struggle to keep on top of
manage to keep on top of
essential to keep on top of
native_notes: Often used when discussing productivity and management style.

usage: Used when describing practical knowledge gained through direct involvement in tasks rather than theoretical study.
example_sentences: I gained valuable hands-on experience during my internship at the engineering firm.
The course is designed to give students more hands-on experience with modern software.
Employers are often looking for candidates who have solid hands-on experience in the industry.
Nothing beats hands-on experience when you are trying to master a new skill.
She has plenty of hands-on experience fixing computer hardware.
native_notes: Very common in CVs and interviews. It highlights that you are a 'doer' rather than a 'thinker'.

uzbek: O'z hissangni qo'shmoq / O'z vazifangni sidqidildan bajarmoq
usage: Used to describe doing your fair share of work in a team setting.
common_mistakes: using it in very formal writing like an academic essay
example_sentences: In a small team, it is essential that everyone pulls their weight to meet the deadline.
If you don't pull your weight, the other members of the group will get frustrated.
He has been struggling to pull his weight since he started the new project.
I feel like I'm the only one pulling my weight around this office.
Everyone needs to pull their weight if we want to finish this task by Friday.
native_notes: Idiomatic expression that sounds very natural in workplace team meetings or performance feedback sessions.
russian: Выполняй свою часть работы/Прилежно выполняй свой долг

usage: Used to express that you are managing your workload effectively and not falling behind.
common_mistakes: saying 'keep on top of things' (also common, but 'stay' is often used for ongoing states)
example_sentences: I use a digital planner to help me stay on top of things at work.
It can be difficult to stay on top of things when you have multiple deadlines.
If you stay on top of things, you won't feel so stressed at the end of the week.
She is very good at staying on top of things, even during busy periods.
Make sure you stay on top of your emails so you don't miss important messages.
native_notes: Focuses on being proactive. Unlike 'keep up with' (which implies reacting to the workload), 'stay on top' implies mastery.

usage: Used to describe a workplace where tasks move quickly and change often.
example_sentences: I enjoy working in a fast-paced environment where no two days are the same.
The retail sector is known for being a very fast-paced environment.
Applicants should be able to thrive in a fast-paced environment.
Working in a fast-paced environment requires excellent organizational skills.
She left her last job because she wanted a change from the fast-paced environment of finance.
native_notes: A staple in job advertisements and LinkedIn profiles. It sounds professional and suggests energy.

usage: Used when someone is new to a job and is starting to understand how things work.
common_mistakes: using 'teach the ropes' instead of 'show someone the ropes'
alternatives: Get to grips with the job
example_sentences: It took me a few weeks to learn the ropes at my new job.
My manager spent the first day showing me the ropes.
Don't worry if you feel confused, you'll learn the ropes eventually.
She is currently learning the ropes of project management.
After learning the ropes, he became one of the most efficient employees.
native_notes: Origins in sailing (managing the ropes of a ship). It is a very common idiom for settling into a role.

uzbek: biror narsani o'rganib qolmoq / tushunib olmoq
usage: Used when you start to understand how to do a new task that was previously difficult or confusing.
example_sentences: I was slow at first, but now I’m finally getting the hang of this software.
Don't worry, you’ll get the hang of the procedures within a few weeks.
It took me a while to get the hang of the new filing system.
Once you get the hang of the controls, the machine is very easy to use.
I’m still getting the hang of the company’s internal communication style.
collocations: need time to get the hang of
native_notes: This implies a process of learning through practice rather than just theoretical understanding.

usage: Used to describe being moved to a higher rank or position at work.
grammar_pattern: Get a promotion / Receive a promotion
common_mistakes: get promoted to a job (instead of 'get a promotion')
example_sentences: He worked hard for years before he finally got a promotion.
If you want to get a promotion, you need to show more initiative.
She hopes to get a promotion to manager by the end of the year.
Many employees feel that staying at one company is the best way to get a promotion.
Getting a promotion is one of the main goals for most junior staff here.
native_notes: Use 'get promoted' (verb) or 'get a promotion' (noun phrase) correctly. Do not say 'get promotion' without the article.

expression: to get the hang of it
usage: Used when you start to understand how to do a new task that was previously difficult.
grammar_pattern: Subject + get + the hang of + it/something
common_mistakes: using 'understand' as a direct synonym for the process
example_sentences: At first, the software was confusing, but I'm finally getting the hang of it.
It takes a few weeks to get the hang of this new system.
Don't worry, you'll get the hang of the procedures soon.
Once you get the hang of it, the work becomes much faster.
She didn't get the hang of the machine until her third day.
collocations: slowly getting the hang of it
eventually get the hang of it
hard to get the hang of
native_notes: Very common in the workplace when training new staff.

usage: Used when starting a new project, business, or venture that requires initial effort and momentum.
common_mistakes: Using it for general daily tasks instead of major projects
example_sentences: We need more funding if we want to get this start-up off the ground.
It took months of preparation to finally get the new marketing strategy off the ground.
The local council is struggling to get the community centre off the ground.
Once we get the core idea off the ground, the rest should be easier.
It’s notoriously difficult to get a business off the ground in this economy.
collocations: struggle to get off the ground
native_notes: Implies a difficult beginning stage where initial energy and resources are required.

expression: to be under a lot of pressure
usage: Used to describe a situation where someone has too much work or high expectations.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + under + a lot of pressure
common_mistakes: to be in a lot of pressure
to have a lot of pressure
example_sentences: She is under a lot of pressure to finish the report by Friday.
I feel like I'm constantly under a lot of pressure at this job.
Medical staff are currently under a lot of pressure due to staff shortages.
Don't put him under a lot of pressure; he's already doing his best.
We are all under a lot of pressure to increase our sales targets.

usage: Used when an employee gets a promotion or a new, more difficult task.
example_sentences: I am ready to take on more responsibility within the company.
She was promoted because she was willing to take on more responsibility.
It can be challenging to take on more responsibility while studying.
The manager asked him to take on more responsibility for the client accounts.
I feel I have outgrown my current role and want to take on more responsibility.
native_notes: Use 'take on' for tasks or responsibilities you agree to start doing.

expression: to work in a fast-paced environment
usage: Common in job interviews or LinkedIn profiles to describe dynamic workplaces like tech or retail.
grammar_pattern: Subject + work + in + a fast-paced environment
common_mistakes: to work in a fast environment
to work in a quick-paced place
alternatives: to thrive in a dynamic workplace
to work in a high-pressure setting
to be in a busy office
example_sentences: I really enjoy working in a fast-paced environment where no two days are the same.
She prefers to work in a fast-paced environment rather than a desk-bound office job.
Are you comfortable working in a fast-paced environment?
The startup culture means you must be able to work in a fast-paced environment.
His previous experience taught him how to thrive in a fast-paced environment.
native_notes: We almost exclusively use 'fast-paced' for professional environments; do not say 'fast environment'.

uzbek: ishni o'rganmoq / yangi joydagi vazifalarni tushunib olmoq
usage: Used when starting a new job and getting used to the duties and procedures.
alternatives: to get the hang of it
to get used to the procedures
example_sentences: I’m still learning the ropes in my new position.
It took me a few weeks to learn the ropes of the accounting software.
Don't worry, you’ll learn the ropes eventually; nobody expects you to know everything on day one.
She helped the new interns learn the ropes during their first month.
After learning the ropes, he became the most efficient employee in the department.
native_notes: Refers to the original meaning of operating a sailing ship; now used exclusively for learning new jobs.
russian: освоить работу/понять задачи на новом месте
